text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise in sadness today on the passing of Robert Hosford. He was a beloved husband, father, pop pop, uncle, great-uncle, and friend. He passed away on Wednesday, November 12. He left behind a legacy of love, laughter, and adventure. Robert was a devoted family man, and anybody who spent ten minutes in a room with him understood that he was the cornerstone of his family, the one who put everybody else's needs in front of his own long before anyone thought to ask him to. His love and support knew no bounds. He would lend a hand. He would listen. That was Robert. His warm smile and his infectious laugh could light up a room, and his sense of humour could turn the toughest day into a memorable one. He was his family's biggest cheerleader. He was proud of them. He celebrated their success. Whether he was cheering on his favourite team or teaching a lesson, his passion for sports was matched only by his love for his family. Please join me in expressing condolences to Robert's family and friends. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. It is with sorrow that I rise today to mark the death of Robert Hosford, a cherished husband, father, pop pop, uncle, great-uncle, and friend. He died on Wednesday, November 12, and what he left behind was a legacy of love, laughter, and adventure. Family came first for Robert; he was its cornerstone, consistently placing the needs of his family ahead of his own. There were no limits to the love and support he gave, and a helping hand or an attentive ear was always available from him. A room would brighten under his warm smile and contagious laugh, and his humour had a way of turning even the hardest day into something worth remembering. He cheered his family on more loudly than anyone, taking pride in what they set out to do and marking every success. His passion for sports, whether he was rooting for his favourite team or passing on a lesson, was rivalled only by his devotion to his family. I ask you to join me in offering condolences to Robert's family and friends. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association are in the gallery today, and several of them sit on the association's Board of Directors. A few of them travelled from as far as Bathurst to get here for two o'clock. Their work holds up mental health and well-being in this province. The association keeps working with the Department of Health, and our system of care is stronger for that. There is more to say about it, and I will say it later today. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to today's opposition motion on the cost of living, on behalf of the good people of Okanagan Lake West—South Kelowna. I would like to inform you that I will be sharing my time with the hon. member for Lethbridge. Today's debate is an important one because it goes directly to the affordability crisis Canadians are living through. Often in this place, along with much of the media, we tend to focus on things we most disagree on. Today I will start with what I hope we can agree on: Canadians are struggling with the rising cost of living. They want practical solutions that lower costs now. That brings me to fuel prices. In recent weeks, Canadians have seen sharp increases in the price of gasoline and diesel. Families felt it immediately, and so did farmers, truckers, tradespeople, small businesses and anyone who depends on transportation. Some will say that global events are to blame, and that may be true, but Canadians do not elect us to describe the problem and then do nothing. They elect us to find solutions. This is why the Conservative official opposition has led the debate on gas prices and affordability, in this chamber and at committee, where we raised the same question before the House rose in December. We are not shrugging our shoulders while Canadians struggle, nor have we simply named the problem, but we have proposed solutions.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in sadness on the passing of Robert Hosford. Robert was a husband, a father, a pop pop, an uncle, a great-uncle, and a friend. He passed away on Wednesday, November 12. What he left behind is love, laughter, and adventure, and I do not think I can improve on that. Robert was a devoted family man. He was the cornerstone of his family and he put their needs before his own, every time. His love and support knew no bounds. He would lend a hand, or he would just listen. His smile and his laugh could light up a room. His sense of humour could turn the toughest day into a memorable one. Anyone who was at the service knows exactly what I mean. He was his family's biggest cheerleader, proud of what they took on and first to celebrate when it went well. Whether he was cheering on his favourite team or teaching a lesson, Robert's passion for sports was matched only by his love for his family. Please join me in expressing condolences to Robert's family and friends. Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate two remarkable authors today, Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck of L'nui Menikuk, which people also know as Indian Island First Nation. They have put out a cookbook called Mitji— Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk, and it speaks to the heritage and the resilience of the people of Mi'gma'gi. But, Mr. Speaker, this is not just a cookbook. The recipes come with the historical knowledge and the lived experience of a community that has been on these lands for generations. The book also takes on gastrocolonialism, which is how colonial policy went in and changed traditional Indigenous recipes. That is not a small thing to write about. I would ask all members to join me in congratulating Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck for the work they have done to preserve Indigenous culinary traditions.

Among our guests are members of the association's board of directors. Their work is essential to the mental health and well-being of New Brunswickers. I will say that again: essential. The association's continued collaboration with the Department of Health is helping to strengthen our system of care, and I look forward to sharing more on that a little later today. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at second reading of Bill C-12, the immigration system and borders act, and I want to pick up where I left off when Bill C-2 was before the House.

The failures do not end there. The Liberals also refuse to acknowledge their abject failure on border security, another critical element that Bill C-12 purportedly aims to address. Earlier this year, the Canada Border Services Agency revealed that 600 foreign criminals were scheduled for deportation, but now they have gone missing in custody. This is completely unacceptable and represents a grave threat to public safety. Canada's border must be secure to protect Canadians from criminals and illegal activities, including fentanyl trafficking and gun smuggling.

Canadians deserve better from their government, one that respects their privacy, does not overreach with warrantless surveillance powers and is serious about fighting fentanyl by imposing real consequences on traffickers. Canadians deserve a government that protects our borders, enforces immigration laws fairly and firmly and supports law enforcement in combatting organized crime, and a government that does not leave foreign criminals at large in our communities. Canadians are looking to this House for leadership, not partisanship, on critical issues like public safety and immigration.

While we have serious concerns about how the government first approached matters in Bill C-2, we also acknowledge that Bill C-12 represents a step in the right direction. This very step came because Canadians raised their voices and the Conservatives did our job: We were listening, we pushed back and we demanded better on behalf of the citizens of this country.

Our work here is not done. We will support moving Bill C-12 to committee, where it will be scrutinized carefully at clause-by-clause, and we will be seeking witnesses from the CBSA on those 600 files. We will work to improve the bill even further before it comes back to this place at report stage.

Mr. Speaker, however, there is an even more troubling pattern here. Under the trade continuity agreement, the U.K. has not been acting fairly toward our pork and cattle producers. The U.K. objects to carcass washes applied at Canadian slaughter plants and opposes the use of growth promotants in beef and pork production. The trade statistics tell the real story of the Liberal government's failure to stand up for our producers. Britain exported over 40 million dollars' worth of beef into Canada in 2024 and nearly 30 million dollars' worth in the first half of 2025. In comparison, Canada exported to Britain just 25,000 dollars' worth in 2024 and, to date, has no beef exports in 2025. For those who are watching, that is 25,000 dollars' worth in 2024, which is unbelievable.

Wade, who runs a cow-calf operation north of Moose Jaw, wrote to my office last month, and I will read what he sent, as he wrote it: We were told for two years that this UK deal would open up a market for us and it has not. Not one pound off this place has gone over there, not one. Meanwhile I walk into the store here in town and there is British beef sitting in the cooler. I would like somebody in Ottawa to explain to me how that is a deal, because from where I am standing it looks like we gave them the shelf space and got nothing back. Those are the words of one producer about his own herd.

This is not fair trade. This is a one-way street that favours British producers, while our farmers and ranchers face non-tariff barriers designed to shut them down. As a mayor, I learned that economic development happens through work, not announcements. We attracted major investment to Moose Jaw by rolling up our sleeves and delivering results, $1.3 billion of results in six years. The U.K. and Canada share more than just a monarch; we share values, institutions and centuries of partnership. From Vimy Ridge to Afghanistan, we have stood together. Now, when it comes to trade, we are making them wait while we sort out our bureaucratic mess. During my time at King's College London, I witnessed Britain's commitment to innovation, enterprise and global engagement, and the U.K.'s decision to join CPTPP represents exactly that forward-thinking approach.

The failures do not end there. The Liberals also refuse to acknowledge their abject failure on border security, another critical element that Bill C-12 purportedly aims to address. Earlier this year, the Canada Border Services Agency revealed that 600 foreign criminals were scheduled for deportation, but now they have gone missing in custody. This is completely unacceptable and represents a grave threat to public safety. Canada's border must be secure to protect Canadians from criminals and illegal activities, including fentanyl trafficking and gun smuggling. Canadians deserve better from their government, one that respects their privacy, does not overreach with warrantless surveillance powers and is serious about fighting fentanyl by imposing real consequences on traffickers. Canadians deserve a government that protects our borders, enforces immigration laws fairly and firmly and supports law enforcement in combatting organized crime, and a government that does not leave foreign criminals at large in our communities. Canadians are looking to this House for leadership, not partisanship, on critical issues like public safety and immigration. While we have serious concerns about how the government first approached matters in Bill C-2, we also acknowledge that Bill C-12 represents a step in the right direction. This very step came because Canadians raised their voices and the Conservatives did our job: We were listening, we pushed back and we demanded better on behalf of the citizens of this country. Our work here is not done. We will support moving Bill C-12 to committee, where it will be scrutinized carefully, and we will work to improve it even further.

Madam Speaker, I stand today feeling both greatly satisfied and deeply grateful. The long-awaited new bridge linking Île Lamèque and Shippagan is finally going to be built. My thanks go to the Premier, Hon. Susan Holt, and to the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure, Hon. Chuck Chiasson, who travelled to the region in February to make the announcement — a turning point for the communities I represent. Once built, the bridge will make getting around easier, tie us more closely to the rest of the province, and open up fresh economic prospects for our people. Speaking for my constituents, I want to thank every person who had a hand in bringing this important project for our community to fruition. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I stand today to mark the lasting importance of the Battle of Vimy Ridge, which took place on April 9, 1917, and which stands among the moments that defined Canada. The Vimy Foundation has worked since 2006 to educate Canadians about that battle and keep awareness of it alive. The campaign being run this year opens the countdown toward 2027, when the battle reaches its 110th anniversary — a landmark date in our country's history. Vimy Week runs from April 2 to April 9, and I would urge every member here to wear the Vimy Pin during it. The pin carries four separate colours, standing for the unity and the sacrifice of the four Canadian divisions that fought side by side for the first time at Vimy Ridge. Wearing it is how we pay tribute to their bravery, what they gave up, and the inheritance they passed on — an inheritance that helped make our nation what it is. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

And I would tell members to go and get the book. Mine already has two pages stuck together.

Madam Speaker, this government introduced a universal breakfast program across every school in New Brunswick this past September. Nearly a year on, the results are already tangible. Students in every part of the province begin each morning with a nourishing meal — milk, eggs, bagels, apples, and cheese. Working in partnership with FeedNB, schools can put healthy food on the table, much of it coming from farms and businesses right here at home. With the cost of living climbing, this program is making a genuine difference for a great many families. It saves parents both time and money and takes some of the pressure off the morning rush. Beyond that, Madam Speaker, it means students arrive in class ready to learn, to focus, and to take part. That is a real investment in our young people's success, because ultimately every child ought to be able to begin the day on the right foot, Madam Speaker. Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, let me say off the top that I will be splitting my time with a great new member, the hon. member for Terra Nova—The Peninsulas. Since this is my first time speaking for a substantive length of time since the election, please allow me to thank the hard-working, industrious people of Flamborough—Glanbrook—Brant North for the honour of being their voice and their servant and for carrying their hopes and dreams to this place. While I have lived and worked in other places in North America in my career, I have always felt and known that the communities of Flamborough—Glanbrook—Brant North are my true home, and home is where the heart is. It is the honour of my lifetime to serve these great communities. I want to thank my campaign team, including Simon, Mona, Jordan, Wendy, Jim and hundreds of volunteers. Above all, I thank my wife, Tracy, without whose love and support I certainly would not be here today. I will now go to the matter at hand. Canadians are struggling, not because we lack talent and not because we lack resources, but because we are too often being held back by red tape, gatekeeping and a government that over-promises and under-delivers. Nowhere is that clearer than when it comes to getting big projects built or trying to move goods and services and workers across provincial lines in our own country. These barriers do not cost us only time and money; they also cost us opportunities, investments and jobs. That is why Bill C-5, an act to enact the free trade and labour mobility in Canada act and the building Canada act, is such a missed opportunity. It claims to deliver free trade and fast-tracked projects, but the reality is it would deliver bureaucratic theatre; it is a showpiece of announcements without the substance to back them up.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to recognize the Battle of Vimy Ridge. It was fought on April 9, 1917. It is one of the defining moments in Canada's history. Since 2006, the Vimy Foundation has worked at raising awareness of that battle and educating Canadians about it, and this year's campaign marks the beginning of the lead-up to the 110th anniversary in 2027, which I hope every school in my riding takes part in, because a date on a page does not mean much to a 14-year-old unless somebody in the room makes it mean something. Vimy Week runs from April 2 to 9. Wear the pin. The Vimy Pin is composed of four distinct colours, one for each of the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge, and it stands for their unity and their sacrifice. That is what we are honouring. Their courage. The legacy they left behind, which helped define this nation. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I am not a cook, and I am not the member anyone should be asking about recipes. I can tell you about a book. Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck, of L'nui Menikuk, also known as Indian Island First Nation, have published Mitji — Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. It is not just a cookbook. The recipes carry the historical knowledge and the lived experience of a community that has thrived on these lands for generations, the people of Mi'gma'gi. I had not heard the word gastrocolonialism before I read it. It is what colonial policies did to traditional Indigenous recipes, and these two authors take it on directly rather than around the edges. Mr. Speaker, I invite all members to join me in congratulating Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck for their commitment to preserving Indigenous culinary traditions.

Under the Liberal government, there is a two-tier tax code for Canadians. There is one for the rich Liberal friends of the Prime Minister and another for everyone else. Worse yet, in this costly Liberal budget, the Liberal Prime Minister gave himself and his buddies a tax break on the purchase of luxury yachts and private jets, while voting against scrapping taxes on food and groceries. The Liberal Prime Minister helped design a tax system he did not have to live under because he was living outside of it. While Brookfield was safely storing profits in Bermuda, small charities and family businesses faced the full force of the Liberal tax-collecting agency. On top of egregious tax avoidance, the Liberal Prime Minister's conflict of interest cover-up is even worse. Brookfield's chief operating officer confirmed this month that 95% of its companies are not covered by the so-called ethics screen. That means 1,900 companies stand to benefit from government decisions that will enrich the Prime Minister personally at the expense of taxpayers, and Canadians will be kept in the dark about how those companies are involved. The Liberal Prime Minister is even taking private meetings with Brookfield executives at the Prime Minister's Office and while he travels overseas. With ethics like this, how can Canadians trust him? He is starting to look a lot like the last Liberal prime minister, just more costly. At the end of the day, Canadians deserve a prime minister whose loyalty is to the public, not to his private portfolio or the shareholders of Brookfield. Canadians feel betrayed. Do we continue down the path of manipulated budgets, rising debt, shrinking paycheques and declining prosperity, or do we rebuild a country where the numbers are honest, the budgets are responsible and the promise of Canada, that hard work leads to an affordable home, opportunity and security, is restored?

Madam Speaker, it was with deep sadness that I learned of the passing of Roméo H. LeBlanc at the age of 102. He was an Acadian veteran of the Second World War. I won't stand here and claim I knew him well, because I didn't. As Minister responsible for Military Affairs, I want to pay tribute to him for his exceptional service to our country. Beyond his military commitment, Mr. LeBlanc gave his life to supporting the veterans' community and preserving the memory of those who had served. I have met a few people who do that work, and I still don't fully understand where they find the stamina for it. His remarkable journey, marked by courage, devotion, and a deep sense of duty, will be a source of inspiration for current and future generations. On behalf of the government of New Brunswick, I extend my sincerest condolences to his family, his loved ones, and the entire veterans' community. We will remember him. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in sadness on the passing of Robert Hosford — beloved husband, father, pop pop, uncle, great-uncle, and friend. Robert passed away on Wednesday, November 12. I did not know him as well as many people in his community did, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. But I know what they have told me since. He left behind a legacy of love, laughter, and adventure. So much of what I heard came back to the same thing: he was the cornerstone of his family, a devoted family man who put their needs before his own. His love and support knew no bounds. He was always there to lend a helping hand or offer a listening ear. I am told his warm smile and his infectious laugh could light up a room, and that his sense of humour could turn even the toughest day into a memorable moment. Well, he was his family's biggest cheerleader too, proudly supporting their endeavours and celebrating their successes. Cheering on his favourite team, or teaching a lesson — I don't know which one he loved more. His passion for sports was only matched by his love for his family. Please join me in expressing condolences to Robert's family and friends. Thank you.

That is what Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck take on in Mitji — Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. They are from L'nui Menikuk, also known as Indian Island First Nation, and what they have made is an exceptional cultural contribution. Madam Speaker, my colleague raised homelessness in Moncton in this House last week, and I want to put a name beside it. Charlie Burrell.

In Little River, Charlie has given his own time and energy to building a facility and small homes for people experiencing homelessness — people who get walked past. He saw his friends on the streets of Moncton. "Friends" is his word, not mine; he uses it every single time, and he does not let you get away with using another one. Instead of turning away, he stepped up. He brings food and clothing, and, more than that, he offers dignity and hope.

He reminds us that homelessness is not just an issue, but a human experience, and that everyone deserves kindness and opportunity. His efforts pull the community in behind him and get other people involved.

Thank you, Charlie. You care so much.

This arose from a court ruling, a superior court ruling in Ontario. People do not really know this, but a superior court is a lower court. It is not the Supreme Court, as one of my colleagues on the other side said this morning. It was appealable. It was not a great decision, because this is already dealt with. Although it is not a law, there is a process by which the Minister of Immigration, and one of my colleagues on this side said that this is how it is dealt with currently, can deal with these lost Canadians very easily with her current power. She knows that. The government knows that, but it will not admit it. That is the problem here. The government is doing something here when it already has the tools to address it, and it is widening the whole approach to make sure we are seen to be doing something. Most Canadians would say, “What are you doing, and why are you doing it?” We are opening the door here, for all intents and purposes, for the foreseeable future, confusing everybody and causing problems we are going to have to address one way or another. Canadian citizenship is not just a passport. It is a privilege, a responsibility and a bond to this country. Bill C-3 would weaken that bond by allowing people with minimal ties to Canada to claim the same rights and benefits as those who have lived, worked and contributed here. The minister already has the discretion to grant citizenship in these special cases without any of that, and when her officials appear at the citizenship and immigration committee, I intend to ask them how many such grants have been made since the Ontario decision came down.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. It is with sorrow that I rise today to mark the death of Robert Hosford, a cherished husband, father, pop pop, uncle, great-uncle, and friend. He died on Wednesday, November 12, and what he left behind was a legacy of love, laughter, and adventure. Family came first for Robert; he was its cornerstone, consistently placing the needs of his family ahead of his own. There were no limits to the love and support he gave, and a helping hand or an attentive ear was always available from him. A room would brighten under his warm smile and contagious laugh, and his humour had a way of turning even the hardest day into something worth remembering. He cheered his family on more loudly than anyone, taking pride in what they set out to do and marking every success. His passion for sports, whether he was rooting for his favourite team or passing on a lesson, was rivalled only by his devotion to his family. I ask you to join me in offering condolences to Robert's family and friends. Thank you.

The failures do not end there. The Liberals also refuse to acknowledge their abject failure on border security, another critical element that Bill C-12 purportedly aims to address. Earlier this year, the Canada Border Services Agency revealed that 600 foreign criminals were scheduled for deportation, but now they have gone missing in custody. This is completely unacceptable and represents a grave threat to public safety. Canada's border must be secure to protect Canadians from criminals and illegal activities, including fentanyl trafficking and gun smuggling. Canadians deserve a government that respects their privacy. Canadians deserve a government that does not overreach with warrantless surveillance powers. Canadians deserve a government that is serious about fighting fentanyl by imposing real consequences on traffickers. Canadians deserve a government that protects our borders. Canadians deserve a government that enforces immigration laws fairly and firmly. Canadians deserve a government that supports law enforcement in combatting organized crime and does not leave foreign criminals at large in our communities. Canadians are looking to this House for leadership, not partisanship, on critical issues like public safety and immigration. While we have serious concerns about how the government first approached matters in Bill C-2, we also acknowledge that Bill C-12 represents a step in the right direction. This very step came because Canadians raised their voices and the Conservatives did our job. We were listening, we pushed back and we demanded better on behalf of the citizens of this country. Our work here is not done. We will support moving Bill C-12 to committee, where it will be scrutinized carefully, and we will work to improve it even further.

Madam Speaker, Charlie Burrell shows in a striking way just how much difference a single individual can make in their community. Over in Little River, he has poured his time and effort into constructing a facility along with small homes for people living without shelter — people who tend to be overlooked and forgotten. Seeing his friends, as he invariably calls them, homeless on Moncton's streets, Charlie did not look the other way; he stepped forward with compassion. Food and clothing and other necessities are part of what he supplies, but what matters more is the dignity and hope he extends. Through him we are reminded that homelessness is a human experience rather than merely an issue, and that kindness and opportunity are owed to everyone. His work draws the community together and prompts others to pitch in and do some good themselves. What Charlie demonstrates is that change begins when one person decides to care. Thank you, Charlie. You care so much.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on behalf of the good people of Okanagan Lake West—South Kelowna. I would like to inform you that I will be sharing my time with the hon. member for Lethbridge. Today's debate is an important one because it goes directly to the affordability crisis Canadians are living through. Often in this place, along with much of the media, we tend to focus on things we most disagree on. Today I will start with what I hope we can agree on: Canadians are struggling with the rising cost of living. They want practical solutions that lower costs now. That brings me to fuel prices. In recent weeks, Canadians have seen sharp increases in the price of gasoline and diesel. Families felt it immediately, and so did farmers, truckers, tradespeople, small businesses and anyone who depends on transportation. Some will say that global events are to blame, and that may be true, but Canadians do not elect us to describe the problem and then do nothing. They elect us to find solutions. This is why the Conservative official opposition has led the debate on gas prices and affordability. We are not shrugging our shoulders while Canadians struggle, nor have we simply named the problem, but we have proposed solutions.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I want to welcome members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association, who are with us in the gallery. Several of them sit on the association's board of directors. The association keeps working with the Department of Health, and that work is strengthening our system of care. I will have more to say about it later today. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, last September our government launched a universal breakfast program in all New Brunswick schools. Not some schools. I will say that again: all New Brunswick schools. Close to a year later, we are already seeing concrete results. Every morning, throughout the province, students start their day with a nutritious meal: milk, eggs, bagels, apples, and cheese. Through our partnership with FeedNB, schools are able to offer healthy foods, which are often sourced from our local farms and businesses. For many families, especially with the rising cost of living, this program is making a real difference. It saves parents time and money and reduces stress in their morning routine. And it means students come to class prepared to learn. That is the whole point of it, and I am going to repeat it because it gets lost in the arguing about the cost: students come to class prepared to learn. Every child deserves to start their day on the right foot, Madam Speaker. Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck of L'nui Menikuk have written a cookbook. It is called Mitji — Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. I have a copy on the counter at home. However, there is an even more troubling pattern here. Under the trade continuity agreement, the U.K. has not been acting fairly toward our pork and cattle producers. The U.K. objects to carcass washes applied at Canadian slaughter plants and opposes the use of growth promotants in beef and pork production. The trade statistics tell the real story of the Liberal government's failure to stand up for our producers. Britain exported over 40 million dollars' worth of beef into Canada in 2024 and nearly 30 million dollars' worth in the first half of 2025. In comparison, Canada exported to Britain just 25,000 dollars' worth in 2024 and, to date, has no beef exports in 2025. For those who are watching, that is 25,000 dollars' worth in 2024, which is unbelievable. This is not fair trade. This is a one-way street that favours British producers, while our farmers and ranchers face non-tariff barriers designed to shut them down. As a mayor, I learned that economic development happens through work, not announcements. We attracted major investment to Moose Jaw by rolling up our sleeves and delivering results, $1.3 billion of results in six years, not by staging photo ops but by standing up for our community and for our businesses. The government has forgotten that lesson. The U.K. and Canada share more than just a monarch; we share values, institutions and centuries of partnership. From Vimy Ridge to Afghanistan, we have stood together. Now, when it comes to trade, we are making them wait while we sort out our bureaucratic mess. During my time at King's College London, I witnessed Britain's commitment to innovation, enterprise and global engagement. The U.K.'s decision to join CPTPP represents exactly that forward-thinking approach. Meanwhile, Canada is dragging its feet like we are still debating whether trade is good for the economy.

Madam Speaker, I was deeply saddened to hear that Roméo H. LeBlanc, an Acadian who served in the Second World War, has died at 102. In my capacity as Minister responsible for Military Affairs, I rise to honour the outstanding service he gave this country. His contribution went well past his time in uniform: he devoted his life to standing behind the veterans' community and to keeping alive the memory of those who served. Courage, devotion, and a profound sense of duty marked his remarkable life, and it will go on inspiring generations now and to come. Speaking for the government of New Brunswick, I offer my deepest sympathies to his family, to those close to him, and to veterans everywhere. He will not be forgotten. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to Bill C-5, an act to enact the free trade and labour mobility in Canada act and the building Canada act, at the second reading stage, and I will be splitting my time with a great new member, the hon. member for Terra Nova—The Peninsulas. Since this is my first time speaking for a substantive length of time since the election, please allow me to thank the hard-working, industrious people of Flamborough—Glanbrook—Brant North for the honour of being their voice and their servant and for carrying their hopes and dreams to this place. While I have lived and worked in other places in North America in my career, I have always felt and known that the communities of Flamborough—Glanbrook—Brant North are my true home, and home is where the heart is. It is the honour of my lifetime to serve these great communities. I want to thank my campaign team, including Simon, Mona, Jordan, Wendy, Jim and hundreds of volunteers. Above all, I thank my wife, Tracy, without whose love and support I certainly would not be here today. I will now go to the matter at hand. Canadians are struggling, not because we lack talent and not because we lack resources, but because we are too often being held back by red tape, gatekeeping and a government that over-promises and under-delivers. Nowhere is that clearer than when it comes to getting big projects built or trying to move goods and services and workers across provincial lines in our own country. These barriers cost us time and money, and they cost us opportunities, investments and jobs. That is why this bill, which the government wants sent to committee before the House rises, is such a missed opportunity. It claims to deliver free trade and fast-tracked projects, but what it would deliver is bureaucratic theatre, a showpiece of announcements without the substance to back them up. Those are the questions I will be putting at committee.

Canadians are looking to this House for leadership, not partisanship, on critical issues like public safety and immigration. While we have serious concerns about how the government first approached matters in Bill C-2, we also acknowledge that Bill C-12 represents a step in the right direction. This very step came because Canadians raised their voices and the Conservatives did our job: We were listening, we pushed back and we demanded better on behalf of the citizens of this country. Our work here is not done. We will vote to send Bill C-12 to committee at the end of this stage, where it will be scrutinized clause by clause, and we will bring amendments there to improve it further.

This arose from a court ruling, a superior court ruling in Ontario. People do not really know this, but a superior court is a lower court. It is not the Supreme Court, as one of my colleagues on the other side said this morning. It was appealable. It was not a great decision, because this is already dealt with. Although it is not a law, there is a process by which the Minister of Immigration, and one of my colleagues on this side said that this is how it is dealt with currently, can actually deal with these lost Canadians very easily with her current power. She knows that. The government knows that, but it will not admit it. That is the problem here. The government is doing something here, but it already has tools to address it, and it is widening the whole approach to this to make sure we are doing something. Most Canadians would say, “What are you doing, and why are you doing it?” It effectively says that we are opening the door here, for all intents and purposes, for the foreseeable future and confusing everybody, causing some problems that we are going to have to address one way or another. Canadian citizenship is not just a passport. It is a privilege, a responsibility and a bond to this country. Bill C-3 would weaken that bond. It would allow people with minimal ties to Canada to claim the same rights and benefits as those who have lived, worked and contributed here.
